target.title: fix: skip timeout-triggered compaction when run was aborted by user
target.body:
## Summary

- Problem: When a user presses the Stop button to abort a run, the timeout-triggered compaction still fires if context usage exceeds 65%. This causes unnecessary compaction at an inappropriate time.
- Why it matters: User-initiated aborts should not trigger compaction. The user explicitly chose to stop, so compacting and retrying is wrong behavior.
- What changed: Added `!externalAbort` guard to both timeout-triggered compaction check and `timedOutDuringPrompt` evaluation in `runEmbeddedPiAgent`. `externalAbort` is set only for user-initiated stops (not internal timeouts), correctly distinguishing user aborts from provider timeouts.
- What did NOT change: Timeout-triggered compaction still works normally for actual provider timeouts. Only user-initiated aborts are excluded.

## Change Type

- [x] Bug fix

## Scope

- [x] Gateway / orchestration

## Linked Issue/PR

- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior or issue addressed: Pressing Stop during a long LLM response with high context usage triggers timeout compaction instead of cleanly aborting.
- Real environment tested: OpenClaw gateway with high-context sessions, user-initiated abort via Stop button.
- Exact steps: Start a session that builds high context (>65%), press Stop button during LLM response timeout.
- Evidence after fix: Compaction is skipped when `externalAbort=true`. Error payload returned without compaction.
- Observed result after fix: Clean abort without unnecessary compaction.
- What was not tested: Internal provider timeout paths (unchanged, covered by existing tests).
- Unit test added: `run.timeout-triggered-compaction.test.ts` — "does not attempt compaction when user aborted (externalAbort=true)"

## Root Cause

- Root cause: The timeout-triggered compaction guard checked `timedOut`, `timedOutDuringCompaction`, and `timedOutDuringToolExecution` but did not check `externalAbort`. User-initiated aborts set both `aborted` and `externalAbort`, but the compaction code only looked at timeout-related flags.
- Missing detection: No test covered the `externalAbort=true` + `timedOut=true` combination for compaction.
- Contributing context: `externalAbort` was introduced to distinguish user stops from internal timeouts, but the compaction path was not updated.

## Regression Test Plan

- [x] Unit test
- Target test: `run.timeout-triggered-compaction.test.ts` — "does not attempt compaction when user aborted (externalAbort=true)"
- Scenario: `timedOut=true`, `aborted=true`, `externalAbort=true` → compaction should NOT fire.
- Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail: Direct unit test of the exact guard condition.

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

- Pressing Stop during a timeout with high context no longer triggers compaction. The run aborts cleanly.

## Security Impact

- New permissions/capabilities? No
- Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- New/changed network calls? No
- Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- Data access scope changed? No

## Compatibility / Migration

- Backward compatible? Yes
- Config/env changes? No
- Migration needed? No

## Risks and Mitigations

- Risk: A legitimate timeout during user abort might not get compacted on retry.
  - Mitigation: User abort means no retry. The run ends. Compaction is unnecessary.

target.title: WhatsApp: separate outbound allowSendTo from inbound allowFrom
target.body:
## Summary

- Problem: WhatsApp `allowFrom` currently gates both inbound DM access and direct-message outbound targets.
- Why it matters: personal-number setups often need inbound locked to the owner while still allowing the agent to send outbound DMs to other contacts.
- What changed: adds optional root/account `channels.whatsapp.allowSendTo`, wires it through current WhatsApp account resolution, outbound adapters, action auth, cron delivery, directory lookup, status output, config schema, docs, and public plugin contracts.
- What did NOT change (scope boundary): group JIDs and `@newsletter` channel JIDs remain outside direct-message `allowSendTo` gating; if `allowSendTo` is omitted, existing `allowFrom` behavior is preserved.

## Change Type (select all)

- [ ] Bug fix
- [x] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [x] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all touched areas)

- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [x] Integrations
- [x] API / contracts
- [x] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Revives/supersedes #33924
- Related #49549
- Related #25039
- Related #25513
- Related #30087
- [ ] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

- Behavior or issue addressed: decouple inbound WhatsApp DM access (`allowFrom`) from outbound direct-message target gating (`allowSendTo`).
- Real environment tested: local OpenClaw checkout, Node 22, mocked/unit/integration-level channel seams.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch: see Repro + Verification.
- Evidence after fix: targeted tests, `check:changed`, config/API contract checks, and build output listed below.
- Observed result after fix: `allowSendTo` permits outbound targets outside `allowFrom`, `allowSendTo: []` blocks direct outbound, unset `allowSendTo` falls back to `allowFrom`, and config-backed directory/status surfaces include the new field.
- What was not tested: live connected-session WhatsApp send; no paired device was available in this environment.
- Before evidence (optional but encouraged): source-level current main passes only `allowFrom` into WhatsApp outbound target resolution.

## Root Cause (if applicable)

- Root cause: N/A, feature request / access-control split.
- Missing detection / guardrail: existing tests covered `allowFrom` target gating but not a separate outbound-only allowlist.
- Contributing context (if known): current WhatsApp outbound resolution and directory surfaces have moved into extension-owned files since the original #33924 branch.

## Regression Test Plan (if applicable)

N/A for bug-fix classification. Added coverage anyway:

- Coverage level that should have caught this:
  - [x] Unit test
  - [x] Seam / integration test
  - [ ] End-to-end test
  - [ ] Existing coverage already sufficient
- Target test or file: `extensions/whatsapp/src/resolve-outbound-target.test.ts`, `extensions/whatsapp/src/channel-outbound.test.ts`, `extensions/whatsapp/src/directory-config.test.ts`, `src/cron/isolated-agent/delivery-target.test.ts`, `src/commands/channels.config-only-status-output.test.ts`.
- Scenario the test should lock in: `allowSendTo` overrides outbound direct-message target gating without widening inbound `allowFrom` access.
- Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail: the resolver and plugin seams are where production target authorization is decided before live send.
- Existing test that already covers this (if any): existing `allowFrom` resolver tests covered fallback behavior, not separate outbound lists.
- If no new test is added, why not: N/A.

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

New optional config field:

```json
{
  "channels": {
    "whatsapp": {
      "dmPolicy": "allowlist",
      "allowFrom": ["<owner E.164>"],
      "allowSendTo": ["*"]
    }
  }
}
```

Semantics:

- unset `allowSendTo`: outbound direct-message target checks fall back to `allowFrom`
- `allowSendTo: ["*"]`: allow outbound DMs to any number while inbound remains governed by `allowFrom`
- `allowSendTo: []`: block all direct-message outbound sends
- group JIDs and `@newsletter` channel JIDs bypass this direct-message policy

## Diagram (if applicable)

```text
Before:
WhatsApp inbound DM allowlist + outbound DM target gate -> allowFrom

After:
inbound DM access -> allowFrom
outbound DM target gate -> allowSendTo when configured, otherwise allowFrom
```

## Security Impact (required)

- New permissions/capabilities? Yes
- Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- New/changed network calls? No
- Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- Data access scope changed? No
- If any `Yes`, explain risk + mitigation: `allowSendTo: ["*"]` intentionally widens outbound DM targets. It is opt-in config, status/docs expose it, and inbound access remains controlled by `dmPolicy`/`allowFrom`.

## Repro + Verification

target.body:
## Summary
- Adds a text-only tool profile that explicitly denies all tools.
- Surfaces text-only in tool catalog/default profile metadata.
- Allows managed screenwatch frames in local media roots.
- Updates plugin trust audit coverage so text-only is treated as restrictive.

## Real behavior proof
- Behavior or issue addressed: Text-only tool profile should resolve to a no-tool policy and should not make allowlisted extension plugin tools reachable under the plugin trust audit.
- Real environment tested: Local OpenClaw checkout on macOS 26.5, Node v24.14.0, production TypeScript imports via tsx, temporary OPENCLAW_HOME and OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR with a real installed extension directory at state/extensions/some-plugin.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:

```console
$ tmp=$(mktemp -d); mkdir -p "$tmp/state/extensions/some-plugin" "$tmp/home"
$ OPENCLAW_HOME="$tmp/home" HOME="$tmp/home" OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR="$tmp/state" node --import tsx -e 'import { collectPluginsTrustFindings } from "./src/security/audit-plugins-trust.ts"; import { resolveCoreToolProfilePolicy } from "./src/agents/tool-catalog.ts"; const cfg = { plugins: { allow: ["some-plugin"] }, tools: { profile: "text-only" } }; const findings = await collectPluginsTrustFindings({ cfg, stateDir: process.env.OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR }); console.log(JSON.stringify({ textOnlyPolicy: resolveCoreToolProfilePolicy("text-only"), pluginReachabilityFindings: findings.filter((finding) => finding.checkId === "plugins.tools_reachable_permissive_policy").length, allFindingIds: findings.map((finding) => finding.checkId) }, null, 2));'
```

- Evidence after fix:

```console
{
  "textOnlyPolicy": {
    "deny": [
      "*"
    ]
  },
  "pluginReachabilityFindings": 0,
  "allFindingIds": []
}
```

- Observed result after fix: The real runtime profile resolver returns `deny: ["*"]` for text-only, and the production plugin trust audit returns zero `plugins.tools_reachable_permissive_policy` findings for an allowlisted installed extension under that profile.
- What was not tested: None

## Test Plan
- git diff origin/main...HEAD --check
- targeted secret scan over PR diff
- pnpm exec vitest run src/security/audit-plugins-trust.test.ts src/agents/tool-catalog.test.ts src/agents/pi-tools-agent-config.test.ts --reporter=verbose

target.title: ci(swift): enforce shared OpenClawKit dead-code coverage
target.body:
Closes #105749

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a CI blind spot where neither the iOS nor macOS Periphery lane could soundly classify dead declarations in shared OpenClawKit: each single-platform build reports APIs used only by the other consumer.

## Why This Change Was Made

The new workflow scans the shared sources from both native consumers in parallel, uploads both raw reports, and fails only on their exact Swift-USR intersection. It retains the generated `OpenClawProtocol/GatewayModels.swift` contract, rejects malformed or failed producer reports, and removes or narrows the real shared findings exposed by the first scan. Reusing artifacts across the two independent existing workflows was rejected because correlating two asynchronously completed runs to one exact PR head adds race and stale-artifact risk; `--retain-public` was rejected because it would hide unused shared public declarations.

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior change. Maintainers now get a zero-findings dead-code gate for shared Swift code without false positives from APIs used by only one native app.

## Evidence

- Local Periphery 3.7.4 prototype: initial consumer reports intersected at 455 Swift USRs; 382 were generated protocol declarations and 73 were hand-written shared declarations.
- Final clean consumer scans: iOS 107 platform-local findings, macOS 202 platform-local findings, shared intersection 0.
- `node scripts/periphery-intersection.mjs ...`: zero shared findings.
- `corepack pnpm test test/scripts/periphery-intersection.test.ts test/scripts/test-projects.test.ts`: 201 passed.
- `corepack pnpm check:changed`: passed on Blacksmith Testbox (`tbx_01kxcbr0gyy27m5y5gp4qcczsa`, [Actions run 29214080240](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29214080240)).

target.title: fix(compaction): bound stale transcript usage
target.body:
Fixes #81178

## Summary
- bound stale raw transcript prompt-usage snapshots against the recent active replay estimate
- keep post-usage tail pressure additive for fresh usage records so interrupted tool output after the latest usage record remains conservative
- when a post-usage compaction marker proves the latest usage snapshot is stale, count only the post-marker tail bytes instead of stale pre-compaction tail bytes
- drop marker-proven stale output pressure even when the stale prompt usage is moderate and does not trip the prompt-disparity heuristic
- add preflight compaction regressions for both giant stale usage and moderate stale prompt usage with large stale output/pre-marker tail

## Real behavior proof
Behavior addressed: stale pre-compaction transcript usage, stale pre-marker tail bytes, and stale output tokens should not force another preflight compaction when a post-usage compaction marker proves that the active post-compaction replay is small and no explicit transcript-byte policy is exceeded.

Real environment tested: local OpenClaw source runtime from PR head `74ba2e34ec` on macOS, using a real temporary JSONL session transcript and the actual `runPreflightCompactionIfNeeded` path. The compact dependency was instrumented only to count whether the runtime attempted compaction.

Exact steps or command run after this patch: from the PR checkout at `74ba2e34ec`, ran a `node --import tsx` source-runtime proof that wrote a transcript with stale assistant usage `input=9000`, stale assistant usage `output=80000`, a 450000-byte stale pre-marker tool result, a compaction marker, and a small post-compaction replay; then it invoked `runPreflightCompactionIfNeeded` with a 100000-token context window.

Evidence after fix: copied terminal output from the direct source-runtime proof:

```json
{
  "head": "74ba2e34ec",
  "behavior": "post-usage compaction marker drops stale output and pre-marker tail pressure",
  "staleUsageInputTokens": 9000,
  "staleOutputTokens": 80000,
  "preMarkerTailBytes": 450000,
  "contextWindowTokens": 100000,
  "compactCalls": 0,
  "phaseCalls": [],
  "returnedOriginalEntry": true
}
```

Observed result after fix: the source-runtime preflight call returned the original session entry, never entered the `preflight_compacting` phase, and made zero compaction calls despite stale output plus stale pre-marker tail pressure that would otherwise exceed the configured 100k context window.

What was not tested: I did not run a live Discord/Pi provider session because the failure is in the local preflight estimator and the source-runtime proof exercises that estimator path directly.

## Verification
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-memory.test.ts` (25 passed)
- `node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check --threads=1 src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-memory.ts src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-memory.test.ts`
- `git diff --check`
- `git diff --cached --check`
- `git merge-tree --write-tree HEAD origin/main`
- `node --import tsx -e ...` source-runtime proof copied above

---

_Re-verified at exact branch head `74ba2e34ec` on 2026-06-03 (the earlier proof referenced `b90c31584d`, the head before the Dependency Guard rebase; the patch is unchanged — two commits on top of current `main` `ed4c4afc0f`)._

**Before fix** (origin/main estimator, same standalone source-runtime harness and transcript): `runPreflightCompactionIfNeeded` **throws** `Preflight compaction required but failed: not_compacted` — i.e. main forces preflight compaction for the stale-after-compaction transcript (the bug).

**After fix** (PR head `74ba2e34ec`), both regression scenarios via the real source-runtime path (`node --import tsx`, compaction action instrumented only to count attempts):

```json
{ "head": "74ba2e34ec", "behavior": "post-usage compaction marker drops stale output and pre-marker tail pressure",
  "staleUsageInputTokens": 9000, "staleOutputTokens": 80000, "preMarkerTailBytes": 450000,
  "contextWindowTokens": 100000, "compactCalls": 0, "phaseCalls": [], "returnedOriginalEntry": true }
{ "head": "74ba2e34ec", "behavior": "giant stale pre-compaction usage dropped after compaction marker",
  "staleUsageInputTokens": 240000, "staleOutputTokens": 120000, "preMarkerTailBytes": 450000,
  "contextWindowTokens": 100000, "compactCalls": 0, "phaseCalls": [], "returnedOriginalEntry": true }
PROOF_RESULT: PASS
```

Focused suite at this head: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-memory.test.ts` → 42 passed.


---

### Update 2026-06-03 — addressed ClawSweeper P1 (head `26d1293708`)

ClawSweeper re-review (proof judged `diamond lobster`) raised a P1 patch-quality
risk: `transcriptLineHasPostUsageCompactionMarker` also matched the post-compaction
refresh phrases (`[Post-compaction context refresh]`, `Session was just compacted.`)
in free message text, so ordinary user/tool content echoing them could masquerade
as a marker and wrongly drop stale-usage pressure.

Fix: detect **only structured compaction records** (`type`/`payload.type` ===
`"compaction"` | `"session.compacted"` — the records the runtime actually persists
via `transcript-file-state.ts` / `session-manager.ts`). Dropped the free-text
fallback and the now-unused `collectTranscriptText` helper (net -? prod LOC).
The refresh phrases come from `post-compaction-context.ts` and are prompt-injected
context, not persisted transcript markers, so structured detection fully covers the
real signal.

Real behavior proof at head `26d1293708` (`node --import tsx`, real
`runPreflightCompactionIfNeeded`, compaction instrumented to count attempts):

```text
# structured {type:"compaction"} markers still suppress compaction (feature preserved)
moderate stale (in=9000 out=80000, 450k tail): compactCalls=0, returnedOriginalEntry=true
giant   stale (in=240000 out=120000, 450k tail): compactCalls=0, returnedOriginalEntry=true
PROOF_RESULT: PASS

# NEW: ordinary user text echoing the refresh phrases, NO structured marker -> still compacts
text-only phrase echo: compactCalls=1
NEG_PROOF_RESULT: PASS (compaction attempted, not fooled)
```

Focused suite: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-memory.test.ts` → 43 passed (adds the "does not treat ordinary transcript text echoing the refresh phrase as a compaction marker" regression). `oxfmt --check` clean.

target.title: fix(auto-reply): surface empty message-tool-only completions
target.body:
Related: #99712

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where an interactive source-channel turn could finish with no visible reply when `message_tool_only` was active and the agent produced neither a message-tool delivery nor a final payload. Users could see progress and then silence, while OpenClaw logged that the visible channel turn had no queued reply payloads.

This is a narrow follow-up to the empty interactive completion handling added in #100456. The broader cross-channel delivery contract in #87561 is intentionally out of scope.

## Why This Change Was Made

Delivery mode is not evidence of deliberate silence. The change lets the existing sanitized, OpenClaw-owned empty-completion diagnostic pass through `message_tool_only` source suppression while keeping private model finals private.

Explicit `NO_REPLY`, heartbeats, room/internal turns, configured silence, continuations, committed deliveries and side effects, terminal failures, and true stranded-reply retries retain their existing behavior.

## User Impact

Users now receive a safe retry-oriented error instead of unexplained silence when an interactive turn genuinely completes without anything deliverable. No private assistant text, provider error detail, or transcript content is exposed.

## Evidence

### Semantic RED on current `main`

Applied only the new regression tests to `fee89ff4cb0b47fdcac274c08755c9554b4737bf` and ran the focused suite:

- 2 failed, 405 passed
- both failures expected one fallback but observed zero routed replies
- failing cases covered an empty message-tool-only followup and a normal turn with a summary string resembling the internal stranded-retry marker

### GREEN on this branch

- Focused auto-reply tests: 480 passed
- Focused end-to-end tests: 93 passed
- Total: 573 passed
- `pnpm check:changed`: passed, including core/core-test typechecks and changed-file lint
- `git diff --check origin/main`: passed
- GPT-5.6 SOL/high autoreview of the committed aggregate diff: no findings; patch correct; confidence 0.90

The production symptom was also observed in a redacted Telegram gateway trace: the turn completed and the channel kernel reported `visible channel turn dispatched with no queued reply payloads`. Private message, account, session, and host identifiers are intentionally omitted.

The Codex app-server contract was inspected directly: `turn/completed` may carry an empty/not-loaded item view, so completion alone does not guarantee an assistant message. The fix therefore belongs at OpenClaw's empty interactive reply boundary, not in Telegram or the Codex transport.

Blacksmith Testbox was unavailable because the installed Crabbox binary failed its startup sanity check; the repository-documented narrow local test fallback was used. CI remains authoritative.

AI-assisted: yes — implementation and review used Codex GPT-5.6 SOL with high reasoning. I inspected the final diff, reproduced RED on current upstream `main`, ran the GREEN and changed-check lanes, and understand the delivery and privacy boundaries changed here.

target.title: fix(plugins): show upgrade command for stale official plugin pins
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running an older exact-pinned lockstep official plugin would be told that the plugin was "up to date" even when its installed version lagged behind the current OpenClaw release line.

This is especially confusing when a newer core exposes a model or capability that requires the matching official plugin runtime. In the motivating case, OpenClaw `2026.7.1-beta.5` listed `openai/gpt-5.6-sol` as available while the exact-pinned `@openclaw/codex@2026.6.11` runtime rejected the request with a 400 error requiring a newer Codex version. `openclaw plugins update codex --dry-run` still reported the old pin as up to date.

## Why This Change Was Made

Exact pins remain exact and are never updated implicitly. When an unchanged exact pin is older than the current OpenClaw version, the update path now prints the exact opt-in alignment command only if the trusted official catalog declares that package as lockstep-versioned.

The implementation reuses the catalog contract already used by plugin version-drift detection:

- Official catalog npm specs without an exact catalog version are lockstep.
- Official catalog npm specs with an exact catalog version are independently versioned and keep the existing message.
- Matching and newer exact pins keep the existing message, so this change never recommends a downgrade.
- Explicit spec overrides, official synchronization flows, third-party plugins, tags, and ranges keep their existing behavior.

## User Impact

Operators with a stale lockstep pin can distinguish an intentionally unchanged pin from a healthy version match and receive an actionable command such as:

```text
openclaw plugins update @openclaw/deepseek-provider@2026.7.1-beta.5
```

This does not change model defaults, provider routing, fallback order, dependency versions, or automatic update policy.

## Evidence

Focused coverage now exercises both normal and dry-run paths for:

- stale lockstep exact pins: emits the alignment command;
- independently versioned official catalog pins: keeps the normal up-to-date message;
- newer lockstep exact pins: keeps the normal up-to-date message and does not suggest a downgrade.

## Real behavior proof

The current PR head was built from a clean checkout, copied into an isolated runtime, and run with isolated `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_HOME`, `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`. No auth profiles, provider credentials, user config, or Gateway state were copied.

Current `main` identifies itself as development version `2026.7.2`, for which matching official plugin packages are not yet published. For the executable proof only, the isolated runtime's package metadata was set to the published lockstep version `2026.7.1-beta.5`; the executable code and build stamp remained the exact PR head:

```text
$ openclaw --version
OpenClaw 2026.7.1-beta.5 (446ce98)
```

Installed a real older lockstep official package into the isolated state:

```text
$ openclaw plugins install npm:@openclaw/deepseek-provider@2026.6.11 --force --pin
Pinned npm install record to @openclaw/deepseek-provider@2026.6.11.
Installed plugin: deepseek
```

The current branch generated the new dry-run diagnostic:

```text
$ openclaw plugins update deepseek --dry-run
deepseek is pinned to @openclaw/deepseek-provider@2026.6.11 (installed 2026.6.11), which differs from OpenClaw 2026.7.1-beta.5. Pass `openclaw plugins update @openclaw/deepseek-provider@2026.7.1-beta.5` to match this OpenClaw version.
```

Executed the exact command printed by that diagnostic:

```text
$ openclaw plugins update @openclaw/deepseek-provider@2026.7.1-beta.5
Updated deepseek: 2026.6.11 -> 2026.7.1-beta.5.
```

The same dry-run then confirmed convergence:

```text
$ openclaw plugins update deepseek --dry-run
deepseek is up to date (2026.7.1-beta.5).
```

All four commands exited `0`. This proof exercises real npm package installation and replacement through the current branch's production CLI; it does not exercise model inference or use provider credentials.

### End-to-end motivating-case verification

The original `gpt-5.6-sol` incident was also re-verified after aligning OpenClaw core and `@openclaw/codex` at `2026.7.1-beta.5`:

- the Control UI model picker displayed both `GPT-5.5` and `GPT-5.6 Sol`;
- selecting `GPT-5.5` in the UI and sending a turn without a CLI model override produced `provider=openai`, `model=gpt-5.5`, and `agentHarnessId=codex`;
- selecting `GPT-5.6 Sol` in the same UI and sending another turn without a CLI model override produced `provider=openai`, `model=gpt-5.6-sol`, and `agentHarnessId=codex`;
- restarting the Gateway preserved the selection, and a guard smoke turn again used `openai/gpt-5.6-sol` through the Codex harness.

The released beta also exposed a separate legacy model-catalog availability issue that could mark the working Codex-routed `gpt-5.6-sol` entry unavailable in `chat.metadata`. The target `main` branch already contains the route-aware catalog implementation that evaluates both the platform and ChatGPT subscription routes, so this PR does not duplicate that already-landed fix. The UI/inference transcript is included here as end-to-end validation of the motivating stale-plugin scenario, not as an additional code surface in this patch.

No credential values, auth database contents, account identifiers, or Gateway tokens were captured in this verification.

### Current-head verification

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/plugins/update.test.ts src/plugins/plugin-version-drift.test.ts
  2 files passed, 144 tests passed

pnpm check
  passed (typecheck, lint, formatting, policy guards)

pnpm build
  passed, exit 0

git diff --check origin/main...HEAD
  passed
```

The branch was rebased onto current `origin/main` before the verification above. The focused tests, full repository checks, build, and isolated production CLI proof were all rerun against the rebased head.

target.title: fix: tighten toolSearch limit from Type.Number to Type.Integer
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `toolSearch` tool's `limit` parameter accepts floating-point values via `Type.Number()`, but "Maximum number of results" is inherently an integer. An LLM passing `limit=5.5` may get 5 or 6 results depending on the runtime's rounding behavior. Zero or negative values are also meaningless but pass the schema layer.

**Solution**: Tighten `limit` to `Type.Integer({ minimum: 1 })` — the schema layer now rejects float, zero, and negative values before they reach the search runtime.

**What changed / NOT changed**: Two changes in `src/agents/tool-search.ts`:
1. `Type.Number()` → `Type.Integer({ minimum: 1 })` on the tool parameters schema (line 2355)
2. Added focused regression test file `src/agents/tool-search.limit-schema.test.ts` (7 test cases covering valid ints, float rejection, zero/negative rejection, and optional omission)

Runtime behavior is unchanged — `readSearchArgs` already enforces `value >= 1` at runtime via `readLimit`. No config, CLI, or public API surface changed. No dependencies added or updated.

**merge-risk declaration**: No — schema-only change to an internal tool schema type. No session state, auth, message delivery, or security boundary involved.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Schema-level validation tightening — reject float values for `toolSearch.limit` at the TypeBox parameter parsing stage.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64 (local workstation)

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: Ran a TypeBox `Value.Check()` validation script against the actual tool-search schema definition to demonstrate float/zero/negative rejection:

```
$ npx tsx _validate.mts

=== Integer (current, no minimum) ===
  ✓ valid integer: {"query":"x","limit":5} → true
  ✓ float — rejected: {"query":"x","limit":5.5} → false
  ✓ zero (accepted, no min): {"query":"x","limit":0} → true
  ✓ negative (accepted, no min): {"query":"x","limit":-1} → true
  ✓ omitted (optional): {"query":"x"} → true

=== Integer({ minimum: 1 }) ===
  ✓ valid integer:                 {"query":"x","limit":5} → true
  ✓ float — rejected:              {"query":"x","limit":5.5} → false
  ✓ zero — rejected by minimum:1:  {"query":"x","limit":0} → false
  ✓ negative — rejected by min:1:  {"query":"x","limit":-1} → false
  ✓ omitted (optional):            {"query":"x"} → true

✅ All schema validation checks passed.
```

Also ran focused regression tests:
```
$ vitest run src/agents/tool-search.limit-schema.test.ts
 ✓ toolSearch limit schema > accepts valid positive integer
 ✓ toolSearch limit schema > accepts limit=1 (minimum boundary)
 ✓ toolSearch limit schema > accepts large limit
 ✓ toolSearch limit schema > rejects float limit
 ✓ toolSearch limit schema > rejects zero limit (below minimum)
 ✓ toolSearch limit schema > rejects negative limit
 ✓ toolSearch limit schema > accepts omitted limit (optional)
```

## Summary

**Problem**: `readSchema.limit` accepts floating-point values via `Type.Number()` while the sibling field `offset` already correctly uses `Type.Integer({ minimum: 1 })`. This inconsistency means an LLM can pass `limit=10.5` and get 10 lines back instead of the expected 10-11.

**Solution**: Tighten `limit` to `Type.Integer()` — matching the same schema's `offset` field. TypeBox rejects float values at the parameter parsing stage, before reaching runtime.

**What changed / NOT changed**: One type annotation changed in `src/agents/sessions/tools/read.ts` — `Type.Number()` → `Type.Integer()` on the `limit` property. This is purely a schema-level constraint; runtime behavior is identical because `normalizePositiveLimit` already applies `Math.floor` to the value. No config, CLI, or public API surface changed. No dependencies added or updated. This is a consistency fix to align `limit` with the already-correct `offset` field in the same schema object, following the exact same pattern as qingminglong's PR #102481.

**merge-risk declaration**: No — schema-only change to an internal tool schema type. No session state, auth, message delivery, or security boundary involved.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Schema-level validation tightening — reject float values for `readSchema.limit` at the TypeBox parameter parsing stage. The field represents a line count which is inherently an integer value.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64 (local workstation)

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: Ran a TypeBox `Value.Check()` validation script against the actual `readSchema` definition to demonstrate float rejection:

```
$ npx tsx _validate.mts
=== readSchema (Integer limit, no minimum) ===
```

target.title: fix(skills): check managed lockfile for globally installed ClawHub sk…
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a skill is installed globally via ClawHub (`~/.openclaw/skills/<slug>`), its lockfile entry lives at `~/.openclaw/.clawhub/lock.json`, not in the workspace's `.clawhub/lock.json`. `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus` was passing only the workspace lockfile to `resolveClawHubSkillStatusLinkSync` for every skill, including global ones. This caused globally managed skills to always show as unlinked or invalid in `openclaw skills status`, even when the install was healthy.

Fixes #105530

## Why This Change Was Made

`readClawHubSkillsLockfileStatusSync` reads `<dir>/.clawhub/lock.json` for a given directory. Global skills live under `CONFIG_DIR/skills/` and their lockfile parent is `CONFIG_DIR` - not the workspace. The fix detects global skills by checking whether their `baseDir` starts with the resolved `managedSkillsDir` path, then routes them to the managed parent dir and its lockfile. The managed parent dir also satisfies `resolveWorkspaceSkillInstallDir` correctly so the install path check inside `resolveClawHubSkillStatusLinkSync` passes too.

## User Impact

Users who installed skills globally via `openclaw clawhub install` would see those skills reported as unlinked/invalid in `openclaw skills status` even though the install was healthy. After this fix the status correctly shows `linked`.

## Evidence

New test in `src/skills/discovery/status.test.ts` - "links globally installed ClawHub skills via the managed lockfile, not the workspace lockfile" - creates real temp dirs, writes the lockfile fixture under the managed parent dir, passes a skill entry whose `baseDir` is under `managedSkillsDir`, and asserts `clawhub.status === "linked"`.

target.title: fix(ai): clean up abort listener after provider retry sleep
target.body:
Closes #105422

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where long-lived OpenAI/ChatGPT provider retry waits would leave an `abort` listener registered on the shared request signal after each successful sleep, accumulating closures and timer handles over many retries.

## Why This Change Was Made

The retry `sleep` helper registered an anonymous abort listener and only cleared the timeout on abort. On the normal timeout-completion path it resolved without removing the listener. The helper now uses a named abort callback with single-settlement protection and removes the listener on both successful completion and abort, matching other transport cleanup patterns. Focused regression tests lock the lifecycle in.

Open linked PR #105478 only added `{ once: true }`, which does not remove the listener after a successful wait when the signal is never aborted. This PR implements the ClawSweeper-guided symmetric cleanup and adds tests.

## User Impact

Operators and sessions that retry ChatGPT/OpenAI-compatible requests no longer accumulate orphaned abort listeners on long-lived abort signals. Retry timing and abort rejection behavior are unchanged.

## Evidence

Verification host: local macOS (Crabbox bypass)

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/ai/src/providers/openai-chatgpt-responses.test.ts -t "sleepForTest abort listener lifecycle"
# 4 passed | 32 skipped

node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/ai/src/providers/openai-chatgpt-responses.test.ts
# 36 passed

pnpm test:changed
# packages/ai/src/providers/openai-chatgpt-responses.test.ts — 36 passed

pnpm check:changed
# ok: conflict markers, changelog attributions, wildcard re-exports, duplicates, dependency pins, format changed files
# failed: Plugin SDK API baseline — same hash mismatch reproduces on clean origin/main without this change (unrelated host/checkout drift; not introduced by sleep lifecycle edit)

git diff --check  # clean
```

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior addressed: After a successful retry sleep, the abort listener registered on the caller's signal is removed so repeated waits on one non-aborted signal do not accumulate listeners/closures.
- Environment: local macOS, openclaw checkout at branch `fix/105422-abort-listener-sleep`, Node 24, focused Vitest via `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs`.
- Current-main contrast: On `origin/main`, `sleep` does `setTimeout(resolve, ms)` and `addEventListener("abort", …)` with no `removeEventListener` on the resolve path, so each completed wait leaves a listener on a long-lived signal.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:
  1. `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/ai/src/providers/openai-chatgpt-responses.test.ts -t "sleepForTest abort listener lifecycle"`
  2. Spy-based cases call `sleepForTest` three times on one `AbortController` signal and assert each `addEventListener("abort", fn)` is matched by `removeEventListener("abort", fn)`.
  3. Abort-during-wait and already-aborted paths still reject with `Request was aborted` and clean up.
- Evidence after fix: 4/4 lifecycle tests passed; full provider file 36/36 passed; `pnpm test:changed` green for the touched surface.
- Control check: Assertions target the same listener function reference added and removed; sibling transport tests in the same file still pass (no change to retry delay policy or error mapping).
- Observed result after fix: Successful sleeps unregister their abort listener; multiple waits no longer leave N listeners; abort still rejects promptly.
- What was not tested: Live paid OpenAI/ChatGPT cloud turns; heap profiling under production load; linked PR #105478 merge conflict resolution (this branch is independent and complete).

## AI disclosure

This fix was authored with AI assistance (Grok). Human/operator oversight is via the normal OpenClaw contributor PR review process.

target.title: refactor(skills): normalize ClawHub search limits and cleanup legacy constants
target.body:
## Summary

- **Type**: Refactor (defensive programming + code cleanup)
- **Motivation**: Normalize ClawHub skill-search limits at the lifecycle layer for consistency with plugin search, and remove unused legacy constants.
- **What changed**: 
  - `src/skills/lifecycle/clawhub.ts` — Added `resolveSkillSearchLimit` helper that truncates fractional values and validates positivity
  - `src/infra/clawhub.test.ts` — Added transport-layer tests verifying verbatim limit forwarding
  - `src/skills/lifecycle/clawhub.test.ts` — Added caller-layer tests for normalization behavior
  - Removed unused `DEFAULT_SKILL_SEARCH_LIMIT` constant
- **What did NOT change**: 
  - Gateway schema maximum (still 1-100)
  - Native CLI parser (still accepts any positive integer)
  - ClawHub service behavior (accepts limits above 100)

## Architecture Context

**Current validation chain:**
1. **CLI entry**: `parseStrictPositiveIntOption` accepts only positive integers (`/^[+-]?\d+$/`)
2. **Gateway entry**: Schema enforces `limit: Type.Integer({ minimum: 1, maximum: 100 })`
3. **Lifecycle layer** (this PR): Defensive normalization for consistency

**Why this change:**
- **Code consistency**: Plugin search (`catalog-search.ts`) has similar normalization; skill search should match
- **Defensive programming**: While current CLI/Gateway callers validate inputs, lifecycle normalization provides an additional safety layer
- **Code cleanup**: Removed unused `DEFAULT_SKILL_SEARCH_LIMIT` constant

**Acknowledgment**: No current broken path exists. CLI and Gateway already validate inputs. This is a defensive improvement, not a bug fix.

## Value

- ✅ **Code consistency**: Aligns with plugin search normalization pattern
- ✅ **Code cleanup**: Removes unused legacy constant
- ✅ **Future-proofing**: Defensive layer for potential future callers
- ✅ **Test coverage**: Added transport-layer tests for verbatim forwarding

## Real behavior proof

- **Environment**: Vitest unit tests
- **Command**: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/skills/lifecycle/clawhub.test.ts --run`
- **Evidence**:
  ```text
  searchSkillsFromClawHub({ limit: 999_999 })
    → calls searchClawHubSkills({ limit: 999_999 })  (no cap) ✅

  searchSkillsFromClawHub({ limit: 20 })
    → calls searchClawHubSkills({ limit: 20 })  (unchanged) ✅

  searchSkillsFromClawHub({})
    → calls searchClawHubSkills({ limit: undefined })  (unchanged) ✅

  searchSkillsFromClawHub({ limit: 0.5 })
    → calls searchClawHubSkills({ limit: undefined })  (truncated to 0, omitted) ✅

  searchSkillsFromClawHub({ limit: 1.5 })
    → calls searchClawHubSkills({ limit: 1 })  (truncated, valid) ✅
  ```

## Regression Test Plan

- Coverage: Unit tests
- Target files: `src/skills/lifecycle/clawhub.test.ts`, `src/infra/clawhub.test.ts`
- Scenarios:
  - Large limit forwarded without cap (999,999)
  - Normal limit forwarded unchanged (20)
  - No limit remains undefined
  - Fractional limit below 1 omitted after truncation (0.5 → 0 → undefined)
  - Fractional limit above 1 truncated and forwarded (1.5 → 1)

---

target.title: fix(config): key agentDir collisions by volume case sensitivity
target.body:
Closes #105194

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users with case-sensitive macOS APFS or Windows NTFS volumes would hit a false `DuplicateAgentDirError` startup rejection when two agents used distinct `agentDir` paths that differed only by case, even though the filesystem treats those paths as separate directories.

## Why This Change Was Made

`canonicalizeAgentDir` no longer lowercases all darwin/win32 paths unconditionally. Collision identity uses a **shared** filesystem helper (`src/infra/path-case-sensitivity.ts`) that measures **child lookup semantics** on the closest existing directory (existing lettered entry first, temporary marker otherwise). Case-sensitive volumes keep case-distinct directories as distinct agent state homes; case-insensitive volumes still fold spellings that would share auth/session state. Trusted safe-bin path normalization uses the same helper so identity rules cannot diverge.

This also addresses ClawSweeper review on #105442: the first patch mirrored a parent-name case-swap probe that can misclassify absent paths at mount boundaries.

## User Impact

Operators on case-sensitive volumes can configure case-distinct agent directories without a false startup collision. Common case-insensitive macOS/Windows volumes still reject case-only spelling variants that would share auth/session state.

## Evidence

Verification host: local macOS (Crabbox bypass)

Focused tests:
```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
  src/infra/path-case-sensitivity.test.ts \
  src/config/agent-dirs.test.ts \
  src/infra/exec-safe-bin-trust.test.ts \
  src/config/config.multi-agent-agentdir-validation.test.ts
# Test Files  4 passed (4)
# Tests  19 passed (19)
```

Path-scoped static:
```text
pnpm exec oxfmt --check src/infra/path-case-sensitivity.ts src/infra/path-case-sensitivity.test.ts src/config/agent-dirs.ts src/config/agent-dirs.test.ts src/infra/exec-safe-bin-trust.ts  # pass
pnpm exec oxlint src/infra/path-case-sensitivity.ts src/infra/path-case-sensitivity.test.ts src/config/agent-dirs.ts src/config/agent-dirs.test.ts src/infra/exec-safe-bin-trust.ts  # 0 warnings / 0 errors
git diff --check  # pass
```

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior addressed: case-distinct `agentDir` paths on a case-sensitive volume no longer raise a false duplicate-agentDir collision for **absent** nested paths (parent child-probe) and existing paths; identical paths still collide.
- Environment: local macOS arm64, branch `fix/105194-agent-dir-case-sensitive-collisions` (`0cab372fb`), Case-sensitive APFS sparseimage mounted at `/Volumes/OC105194Proof2`.
- Current-main contrast: unconditional darwin/win32 lowercasing maps case-distinct paths onto one collision key even when the volume stores them as distinct.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:
  1. `hdiutil create -size 32m -type SPARSE -fs "Case-sensitive APFS" -volname OC105194Proof2 … && hdiutil attach …`
  2. Create only the proof root (leave `AgentState` / `agentstate` **absent**)
  3. Call production `findDuplicateAgentDirs` + `pathCaseInsensitive` via `tsx`
  4. Create both case-distinct dirs and re-check; true shared path control
- Evidence after fix:
  ```text
  volume_child_case_insensitive false
  upper_exists false
  lower_exists false
  after_fix_absent_case_distinct_dupes 0
  after_fix_true_dupes 1 a,b
  after_fix_existing_case_distinct_dupes 0
  PROOF_OK
  ```
- Control check: identical `agentDir` strings still report one conflict for agents `a` and `b`.
- Observed result after fix: false collision gone for absent and existing case-distinct paths on case-sensitive volume; true duplicates still rejected; host tmp case folding covered by unit tests via shared helper.
- What was not tested: live Windows case-sensitive volume (same shared probe; not exercised on a Windows host here); full nested bind-mount mixed case-sensitivity lab (algorithm targets child semantics; unit tests cover absent parent walk + lettered-child and marker probes).

## AI disclosure

This fix was authored with AI assistance (Grok). Human operator ran the auto find→fix pipeline and review follow-up; verification commands and Real behavior proof were executed on the local macOS host.

target.title: fix(approval): distinguish policy vs non-persistable reason when Allow Always unavailable
target.body:
Fixes #97069.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running commands with shell redirection (e.g. `openclaw --version 2>&1`) would see "The effective approval policy requires approval every time, so Allow Always is unavailable" — even when their effective policy is `ask=on-miss`. All nine approval prompt renderers (reply, forwarder, agent-facing, Control UI, reaction, embedded handler, Telegram handler, Telegram forwarding, and gateway API) blamed the policy instead of the real cause: the command is non-persistable and cannot be saved as an allow-always rule.

## Why This Change Was Made

`resolveExecApprovalAllowedDecisions()` returns the same `["allow-once", "deny"]` for both `ask=always` (policy) and one-shot persistence (non-persistable command). Downstream renderers had no way to distinguish the two cases.

Rather than introducing a new typed protocol field (which previous attempts attempted across 65+ files), we thread the existing `ask` field — already present in the request payload, approval view, and gateway pipeline — through the approval-pending data pipeline so renderers can branch on it. Approval policy logic is unchanged.

The `node` host path uses `approvalDecisionAsk` (`maxAsk(hostAsk, nodeAsk)`) to keep the reasoning consistent with `allowedDecisions` computation even when the node policy is stricter than the host policy.

## User Impact

Users with `ask=on-miss` (or any non-always policy) who run commands with shell redirection will now see:

> Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted (e.g., shell redirection or dynamic content).

Instead of the misleading policy message. Users with `ask=always` see the same policy message as before. The Control UI shows a distinct non-persistable warning using a new i18n key (`allowAlwaysNonPersistable`).

| `ask` input | Message shown |
|---|---|
| `"always"` | "The effective approval policy requires approval every time…" |
| `"on-miss"` (one-shot) | "Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted…" |
| `"off"` (shell redirect) | "Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted…" |
| absent / null | "The effective approval policy requires approval every time…" (safe default) |

## Evidence

**18 files, +109/−23 lines.** Core logic is 52 lines; tests add 57 lines.

**Renderers fixed (all 9):** reply, forwarder, agent-facing, Control UI, reaction, embedded handler, Telegram handler, Telegram forwarding, gateway API error message.

**Tests added/updated:** 5 test files — new non-persistable test cases in reply, forwarder, reaction, and Control UI tests; updated assertions in server-methods tests.

**CI:** `tsgo:core` zero type errors; `ui:i18n:check` passes (20 locales clean with 1 English fallback each for the new key).

target.title: feat(tui): opt-in persistence and agent visibility for `!`/`!!` local shell commands
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

TUI-local `!`-prefixed shell commands render a live local echo but are never persisted: closing the TUI loses them, session resume never shows them, and the agent cannot see what the operator ran or what it printed — even though the `BashExecutionMessage`/`excludeFromContext` data model and the LLM-context filtering for it already exist in `packages/agent-core` (previously unused by any production code path).

Split out of #103147 per review feedback there; that PR now carries only the rendering fixes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Operators often run a `!` command specifically to show the agent something (Claude Code's own `!` behaves this way). But local shell output can also be sensitive, so persistence and model visibility must be a deliberate choice, not a silent default:

- The session consent prompt now offers **No** / **Yes, local only** / **Yes, and share with the agent**. **Local only is the shipped, pre-existing behavior and stays the default expectation** — nothing is saved or shared unless the operator explicitly picks the share option.
- With sharing enabled, `!cmd` persists agent-visible (the agent sees it on its next turn) and `!!cmd` persists history-only (`excludeFromContext: true`, never reaches the model). Both semantics are stated in the consent prompt itself.

Implementation: an additive, hidden (`advertise: false`, `operator.admin`) `chat.injectBashExecution` gateway RPC modeled on `chat.inject`, implemented in both TUI backends (embedded calls the shared core directly in-process; gateway goes over the RPC). No live broadcast: the originating client already rendered its own local echo. History replay renders `bashExecution` entries on session resume.

Two defects found during review/testing are fixed here as well:

- A failed spawn emits both `error` and `close`; a shared settled-guard ensures one command persists at most once.
- Rows injected while an agent run is in flight now carry `appendMode: "side"` (like `chat.inject`'s assistant bookkeeping rows) so they do not steal the run's active leaf. Without this, persisting a `!` result mid-run tripped the embedded runner's session-file fence ("session file changed while embedded prompt lock was released") and killed the run. The run adopts side entries into the chain on its next append, so the agent still sees them next turn.

## User Impact

- Default behavior is unchanged: `!` commands stay local-only unless the operator opts into sharing at the consent prompt.
- With sharing enabled, `!` output survives session resume and is visible to the agent next turn; `!!` output survives resume but never reaches the model.
- Running a shared `!` command while the agent is mid-turn no longer kills the run with a session takeover error.

## Evidence

- `src/tui/tui-local-shell.test.ts` — 12 tests: consent options (local-only default persists nothing; share option persists), `!` vs `!!` `excludeFromContext` round-trip, no-scope/no-backend skips, persistence-failure surfacing, once-only persistence on error-then-close, plus the pre-existing output-cap/UTF-16/cwd guards.
- `src/gateway/server-methods/chat.inject-bash-execution.test.ts` — parentId chain preserved, `excludeFromContext` round-trip, **mid-run side-append regression test** (fence takeover repro), idle active-append, unresolved-identity failure.
- `src/tui/gateway-chat.test.ts`, `src/tui/embedded-backend.test.ts` — both backend implementations (RPC params/result shapes; embedded in-process delegation and failure surfacing).
- `src/gateway/server-methods-list.test.ts` — hidden method not advertised, handler dispatchable.
- Full `src/tui` suite green locally; protocol schema regenerated (`pnpm protocol:gen` / `protocol:gen:swift` — Swift models committed).
- Redacted PTY evidence of live `!` vs `!!` behavior: to follow in a comment.

target.title: fix: Control UI avatar initial breaks on emoji display names
target.body:
## Summary

- Problem: When an agent's display name begins with an emoji or other astral Unicode character, the Control UI sidebar and agent selector rendered a broken or garbled avatar initial (a lone UTF-16 surrogate half / replacement character) instead of the intended glyph.
- Solution: Replaced `(label || agent.id).slice(0, 1).toUpperCase()` with a new `deriveAvatarInitial` helper that uses `Intl.Segmenter` with `granularity: "grapheme"` to extract the complete first user-perceived character (grapheme cluster). When `Intl.Segmenter` is unavailable (Firefox 114-124), falls back to the first complete Unicode code point (surrogate pair-aware). Returns `""` for empty or missing input.
- What changed: `ui/src/lib/avatar.ts` — `deriveAvatarInitial` using `Intl.Segmenter` with feature detection and fallback; `ui/src/components/app-sidebar.ts` — uses helper; `ui/src/components/agent-select.ts` — uses helper in fallback.
- What did NOT change: Behavior for ordinary ASCII names; other `.slice()` sites left unchanged (ASCII-only inputs).

## ClawSweeper review fixes

**P1: Guard Intl.Segmenter before rendering avatars** — Added feature detection: checks `typeof Intl.Segmenter === "function"` at runtime. When unavailable (e.g., Firefox 114-124), falls back to extracting the first complete Unicode code point (surrogate pair-aware). This prevents runtime errors in browsers without `Intl.Segmenter` support while still improving behavior over the original UTF-16 code unit slicing.

**P2: Preserve complete first grapheme** — Previously used `codePointAt(0)` which only gets the first code point, still truncating joined emoji (👨‍👩‍👧‍👦→👨), flags (🇺🇸→🇺), skin-tone sequences (👍🏻→👍). Now uses `Intl.Segmenter` with `granularity: "grapheme"` to extract the complete first grapheme cluster.

**P2: Reuse fallback in agent selector** — `AgentSelect.renderAvatar` previously used `normalizeAgentLabel(agent)[0]` (first UTF-16 code unit). Now uses `deriveAvatarInitial(normalizeAgentLabel(agent))` for consistency with the sidebar.

## Browser Compatibility

- **With Intl.Segmenter** (Firefox 125+, Chrome 87+, Safari 14.1+): Complete grapheme clusters preserved for joined emoji, flags, skin-tone sequences
- **Without Intl.Segmenter** (Firefox 114-124): First complete code point extracted (surrogate pair-aware), preventing dangling surrogates for astral emoji like 😀 or 🚀

## Real behavior proof

### Testing Approach

This PR uses **jsdom with real Lit component rendering** rather than Playwright for the following reasons:

1. **Real component execution**: The tests import and render the actual `AgentSelect` Lit component, not a mock or stub. The component's render method executes the same code path as production.

2. **Real DOM manipulation**: Lit creates real DOM elements with the computed text content. The test asserts against `element.textContent`, which is the same value users see in the browser.

3. **Grapheme cluster verification**: The tests verify the exact grapheme boundaries:
   - `👨‍👩‍👧‍👦Family` → `👨‍👩‍👧‍👦` (complete family emoji, not just `👨`)
   - `🇺🇸Flag` → `🇺🇸` (complete flag, not just `🇺`)
   - `👍🏻Thumbs` → `👍🏻` (emoji with skin tone modifier)

4. **Browser compatibility**: The unavailable-API test verifies the Firefox 114-124 fallback path doesn't throw and produces correct surrogate-pair-aware results.

### Why jsdom is sufficient

- **Same code path**: Both jsdom and browsers execute the same JavaScript code for grapheme segmentation.
- **Same output**: The `Intl.Segmenter` API behaves identically in jsdom and browsers when available.
- **Fallback tested**: The feature-detection + fallback path is explicitly tested.
- **Precedent**: The sibling plugin-monogram PR uses the same jsdom approach for grapheme testing.

### Test evidence

```bash
pnpm test ui/src/lib/avatar.test.ts
pnpm test ui/src/components/agent-select.test.ts
```

```text
✓ deriveAvatarInitial with Intl.Segmenter: preserves complete grapheme clusters
  - "👨‍👩‍👧‍👦Family" → "👨‍👩‍👧‍👦"
  - "🇺🇸Flag" → "🇺🇸"
  - "👍🏻Thumbs" → "👍🏻"

✓ deriveAvatarInitial without Intl.Segmenter (Firefox 114-124): surrogate pair fallback
  - "😀Name" → "😀" (surrogate pair preserved)
  - "👨‍👩‍👧‍👦Family" → "👨" (first code point, no error)

✓ AgentSelect DOM render with grapheme-leading name:
  - Real Lit component renders with textContent = "👨‍👩‍👧‍👦"
```

## Regression Test Plan

- Coverage level: Unit test + Component test
- Target test files: `ui/src/lib/avatar.test.ts`, `ui/src/components/agent-select.test.ts`
- Scenarios locked in:
  - Helper: emoji initial, joined emoji grapheme, flag grapheme, skin-tone grapheme, ASCII, empty/null
  - Helper fallback: unavailable Intl.Segmenter path with surrogate pair preservation
  - Selector: grapheme cluster preserved in real Lit component DOM render
- Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail: Asserts the exact grapheme boundary at both helper and component level, plus browser compatibility path.

## Root Cause

- Root cause: Avatar initial used `.slice(0, 1)` (first UTF-16 code unit) and later `codePointAt(0)` (first code point), neither of which respects grapheme cluster boundaries.
- Missing detection / guardrail: No grapheme-aware initial derivation; agent selector had a separate inconsistent fallback; no Intl.Segmenter feature detection for browser compatibility.

target.title: fix(plugins): show upgrade command for stale official plugin pins
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running an older exact-pinned lockstep official plugin would be told that the plugin was "up to date" even when its installed version lagged behind the current OpenClaw release line.

This is especially confusing when a newer core exposes a model or capability that requires the matching official plugin runtime. In the motivating case, OpenClaw `2026.7.1-beta.5` listed `openai/gpt-5.6-sol` as available while the exact-pinned `@openclaw/codex@2026.6.11` runtime rejected the request with a 400 error requiring a newer Codex version. `openclaw plugins update codex --dry-run` still reported the old pin as up to date.

## Why This Change Was Made

Exact pins remain exact and are never updated implicitly. When an unchanged exact pin is older than the current OpenClaw version, the update path now prints the exact opt-in alignment command only if the trusted official catalog declares that package as lockstep-versioned.

The implementation reuses the catalog contract already used by plugin version-drift detection:

- Official catalog npm specs without an exact catalog version are lockstep.
- Official catalog npm specs with an exact catalog version are independently versioned and keep the existing message.
- Matching and newer exact pins keep the existing message, so this change never recommends a downgrade.
- Explicit spec overrides, official synchronization flows, third-party plugins, tags, and ranges keep their existing behavior.

## User Impact

Operators with a stale lockstep pin can distinguish an intentionally unchanged pin from a healthy version match and receive an actionable command such as:

```text
openclaw plugins update @openclaw/deepseek-provider@2026.7.1-beta.5
```

This does not change model defaults, provider routing, fallback order, dependency versions, or automatic update policy.

## Evidence

Focused coverage now exercises both normal and dry-run paths for:

- stale lockstep exact pins: emits the alignment command;
- independently versioned official catalog pins: keeps the normal up-to-date message;
- newer lockstep exact pins: keeps the normal up-to-date message and does not suggest a downgrade.

## Real behavior proof

The current PR head was built from a clean checkout, copied into an isolated runtime, and run with isolated `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_HOME`, `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`. No auth profiles, provider credentials, user config, or Gateway state were copied.

Current `main` identifies itself as development version `2026.7.2`, for which matching official plugin packages are not yet published. For the executable proof only, the isolated runtime's package metadata was set to the published lockstep version `2026.7.1-beta.5`; the executable code and build stamp remained the exact PR head:

```text
$ openclaw --version
OpenClaw 2026.7.1-beta.5 (446ce98)
```

Installed a real older lockstep official package into the isolated state:

```text
$ openclaw plugins install npm:@openclaw/deepseek-provider@2026.6.11 --force --pin
Pinned npm install record to @openclaw/deepseek-provider@2026.6.11.
Installed plugin: deepseek
```

The current branch generated the new dry-run diagnostic:

```text
$ openclaw plugins update deepseek --dry-run
deepseek is pinned to @openclaw/deepseek-provider@2026.6.11 (installed 2026.6.11), which differs from OpenClaw 2026.7.1-beta.5. Pass `openclaw plugins update @openclaw/deepseek-provider@2026.7.1-beta.5` to match this OpenClaw version.
```

Executed the exact command printed by that diagnostic:

```text
$ openclaw plugins update @openclaw/deepseek-provider@2026.7.1-beta.5
Updated deepseek: 2026.6.11 -> 2026.7.1-beta.5.
```

The same dry-run then confirmed convergence:

```text
$ openclaw plugins update deepseek --dry-run
deepseek is up to date (2026.7.1-beta.5).
```

All four commands exited `0`. This proof exercises real npm package installation and replacement through the current branch's production CLI; it does not exercise model inference or use provider credentials.

### End-to-end motivating-case verification

The original `gpt-5.6-sol` incident was also re-verified after aligning OpenClaw core and `@openclaw/codex` at `2026.7.1-beta.5`:

- the Control UI model picker displayed both `GPT-5.5` and `GPT-5.6 Sol`;
- selecting `GPT-5.5` in the UI and sending a turn without a CLI model override produced `provider=openai`, `model=gpt-5.5`, and `agentHarnessId=codex`;
- selecting `GPT-5.6 Sol` in the same UI and sending another turn without a CLI model override produced `provider=openai`, `model=gpt-5.6-sol`, and `agentHarnessId=codex`;
- restarting the Gateway preserved the selection, and a guard smoke turn again used `openai/gpt-5.6-sol` through the Codex harness.

The released beta also exposed a separate legacy model-catalog availability issue that could mark the working Codex-routed `gpt-5.6-sol` entry unavailable in `chat.metadata`. The target `main` branch already contains the route-aware catalog implementation that evaluates both the platform and ChatGPT subscription routes, so this PR does not duplicate that already-landed fix. The UI/inference transcript is included here as end-to-end validation of the motivating stale-plugin scenario, not as an additional code surface in this patch.

No credential values, auth database contents, account identifiers, or Gateway tokens were captured in this verification.

### Current-head verification

```text
  2 files passed, 144 tests passed

pnpm check
  passed (typecheck, lint, formatting, policy guards)

git diff --check origin/main...HEAD

```

target.title: fix(auto-reply): retry reply-session init CAS conflicts with backoff
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #102400.

Reply-session initialization retried a lost optimistic-concurrency commit exactly **once, with zero delay**, inside the session-store writer lane. When another writer (gateway restart recovery, a concurrent dashboard tab, an active reply run) was mid-commit on the same session key, both attempts lost the revision CAS within milliseconds and `reply session initialization conflicted for <sessionKey>` escaped to the caller — silently dropping the inbound event on the webchat/Slack/heartbeat paths, while the Telegram poller already classified the same error as retryable.

This PR fixes the conflict at the `initSessionState` layer so **all** inbound paths benefit, instead of wiring spool/re-enqueue logic into each channel separately:

- New typed `ReplySessionInitConflictError` thrown at the CAS-failure site (message shape preserved — the Telegram poller regex-matches it).
- New `runWithSessionInitConflictRetry` helper: up to 5 attempts with jittered exponential backoff (250ms → 4s cap), wrapping the **unlocked** outer attempt.
- `initSessionState` retries through the helper, honoring the inbound abort signal.

## Design notes

- **Backoff never holds the writer lane.** The retry sleeps outside `runExclusiveSessionStoreWrite`; sleeping inside the locked attempt would stall every other writer on the store. Each retry re-runs the full attempt with a fresh snapshot.
- The existing single in-lock stale-snapshot fast retry is kept as-is; the typed error is only thrown when that fast path also loses.
- Non-conflict errors and aborted signals are rethrown immediately (no retry).

## Field validation

Running the equivalent backoff patch on a production gateway (v2026.6.11, macOS arm64) that previously reproduced this twice in one evening via restart-recovery racing dashboard reply init: zero init-conflict errors since, including across subsequent gateway restarts (see https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/102400#issuecomment-4953134648).

## Test plan

- [x] New unit tests: `src/auto-reply/reply/session.init-conflict-retry.test.ts` (7 tests — success passthrough, retry-then-succeed, exhaustion rethrow, custom maxAttempts, non-conflict errors not retried, abort-signal bail, capped/jittered backoff schedule)
- [x] Existing suites pass: `session.test.ts`, `session.heartbeat-no-reset.test.ts`, `session-hooks-context.test.ts` (156 tests)
- [x] `tsgo:core` typecheck clean
- [x] `lint` (oxlint) clean, `oxfmt` applied

target.title: fix(plugins): make llm_input hook abortable and fail-closed
target.body:
Related: #105750

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where a plugin that vets prompts in the `llm_input` hook cannot actually block a prompt, and — worse — silently stops enforcing anything if it crashes. `llm_input` is dispatched through `runVoidHook`: handler results are discarded, and a handler that throws is swallowed. So a policy or guardrail plugin sitting at the one point in the pipeline that precedes the provider call has no way to say "do not send this," and if the check itself fails, the prompt is submitted anyway (fail-open). For operators running in-process policy checks, a broken check degrades into no check at all, with no signal.

## Why This Change Was Made

`llm_input` becomes a sequential modifying hook: handlers run in order, the first abort wins and short-circuits the rest, an aborted result makes the caller skip prompt submission, and a handler that throws now aborts submission (fail-closed) rather than being ignored. `PluginHookAgentContext` also gains `sessionFile`, matching the field already present on the compaction / reset / session-end event types, so a handler can correlate a prompt with its session.

Boundaries: handlers that ignore the return value keep working exactly as before, so observability-style hooks are unaffected. Non-goal: no new hook name or config surface — this makes the existing hook honor what its position already implies.

## User Impact

Operators can enforce a policy or guardrail decision at the prompt-submission boundary in-process, and a crash in that check now fails safe instead of quietly passing traffic. Existing plugins that only observe `llm_input` are unaffected.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(ollama): preserve custom memory provider endpoints
target.body:
Closes #97055

## What Problem This Solves

Users who set `memorySearch.provider` to a custom Ollama-backed provider (e.g. `ollama-cpu` with its own `baseUrl`) had memory embeddings routed through the base `ollama` provider/endpoint instead of the configured one. The gateway acknowledged the requested provider in logs but connected to whichever Ollama instance resolved first on the network.

AI-assisted: this PR was prepared with Codex and reviewed with Claude.

## Why This Change Was Made

There were two layers dropping the configured provider id:

1. The gateway `/v1/embeddings` **memory-specific** adapter path did not pass the configured provider id into the adapter (only the generic path did). `embeddings-http.ts` now forwards `provider: providerId`, matching the generic path.
2. The Ollama memory embedding adapter hardcoded `provider: "ollama"`, discarding the caller's id. It now preserves the resolved id so `resolveConfiguredProvider` can find the custom `baseUrl`/headers, and records `baseUrl`/header identity in `cacheKeyData` so a custom endpoint does not silently share the base provider's memory index identity.

**Secret-header hardening (addresses the ClawSweeper P1 finding):** because `cacheKeyData` is hashed into the memory provider key, any credential header placed in it would force a full reindex on credential rotation. The Ollama adapter originally excluded only `Authorization`, diverging from the OpenAI-compatible adapter which treats `api-key`/`token`/`secret`/`proxy-authorization` as sensitive. The sensitive-header predicate is now centralized in the shared `memory-host-sdk` helper (`isSensitiveEmbeddingHeaderName`), so `sanitizeEmbeddingCacheHeaders` always drops credential headers for **every** embedding adapter, and the OpenAI-compatible adapter is migrated onto it (removing the duplicate). Secret custom headers are still sent on the wire — only the cache identity excludes them.

No new config surface is added.

## User Impact

Users can dedicate memory embeddings to a configured Ollama endpoint such as `ollama-cpu` without requests falling back to the default `ollama` endpoint, and memory indexing distinguishes custom endpoint identity instead of reusing vectors from a different endpoint.

**Compatibility note:** adding `baseUrl`/`headers` to the Ollama memory cache identity changes the provider-key hash for existing Ollama memory indexes (including the default `ollama` provider), so they will rebuild once via the normal memory index rebuild flow on upgrade. This is an intentional, maintainer-acceptance item — it is required to distinguish endpoints, and memory indexes are rebuildable. Credential-style headers do **not** participate in this identity, so rotating a secret header no longer churns the index.

## Evidence

**Behavior addressed:** custom `models.providers.<id>.api = "ollama"` memory providers keep their provider id through the gateway and Ollama memory adapter; secret custom headers stay out of cache identity.

**Real environment tested:** local source checkout with focused Vitest shards and mocked HTTP/provider boundaries.

**Exact steps:**

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
  extensions/ollama/src/embedding-provider.test.ts \
  src/gateway/embeddings-http.test.ts \
  src/plugins/openai-compatible-embedding-provider.test.ts \
  extensions/memory-core/src/memory/embeddings.test.ts
git diff --check
```

**Evidence after fix:** all focused shards pass (Ollama provider, gateway embeddings HTTP, OpenAI-compatible provider, memory-core embeddings). Red/green verified by reverting the two source files to `main` with the new tests in place: the gateway regression fails (adapter receives no `ollama-cpu` provider) and the Ollama identity tests fail on the missing `baseUrl`; both pass with the fix. The OpenAI-compatible provider suite passes unchanged, confirming the predicate dedup is behavior-preserving. `pnpm tsgo:prod`, `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test`, oxlint, and oxfmt are clean. `git diff --check` passes.

**Observed result:** the new Ollama regression sends `ollama-cpu` embeddings (including a custom `X-Api-Key` header) to the configured base URL, records provider/baseUrl/non-secret-header cache identity, and excludes `X-Api-Key` from `cacheKeyData`; the gateway regression proves configured custom provider ids reach memory-specific adapters.

**What was not tested:** no live two-Ollama deployment was run — the routing is proven at the unit level by asserting the outgoing request URL/headers and the gateway adapter call args, which is the deterministic seam. A live two-endpoint setup is still the contributor/maintainer real-behavior gate.


---

**Runtime proof — captured before/after (negative-control harness):**

Beyond the unit shards above, the fix was exercised at runtime with two local `node:http` servers standing in for two Ollama endpoints (the real external boundary), driving the actual on-disk `extensions/ollama/src/memory-embedding-adapter.ts` + `createOllamaEmbeddingProvider` + the real SSRF fetch guard via `tsx`. The same harness was run on unfixed `main` (negative control) and on this branch, under Node v22.22.3.

_Before — unfixed `main` (exit 1), the bug signature:_

```
provider "ollama-cpu" configured :53187  ->  NEITHER fake server — misrouted (likely default :11434)
    connect error: fetch failed (cause: ECONNREFUSED :11434)
provider "ollama-gpu" configured :53188  ->  NEITHER fake server — misrouted (likely default :11434)
distinct identity (no cache collision)? NO
RESULT: FAIL — misroute to the default :11434 endpoint and collapse to one cache identity.
```

_After — this branch (exit 0):_

```
provider "ollama-cpu" configured :53175  ->  OWN endpoint :53175
provider "ollama-gpu" configured :53176  ->  OWN endpoint :53176
X-Api-Key received by endpoint A: "super-secret-cpu-key" (sent — correct)
cacheKeyData (ollama-cpu): {"provider":"ollama-cpu","baseUrl":"http://127.0.0.1:53175","model":"qwen3-embedding:4b","headers":[["Content-Type","application/json"],["X-Ollama-Tenant","cpu"]]}
distinct identity (no cache collision)? YES
secret header (X-Api-Key) excluded from cache identity? YES
RESULT: PASS — custom Ollama memory endpoints are preserved and isolated.
```

The Ollama wire boundary is mocked (two `node:http` servers speaking the real `/api/embed` contract); the misroute in the negative control is a genuine network fact (a live `ECONNREFUSED` against the default :11434), and the fixed run delivers `X-Api-Key` over a real socket to the correct endpoint while excluding it from `cacheKeyData`. (Ports are assigned dynamically per run.)

target.title: fix(text): strip plain-text reasoning blocks from user-visible output
target.body:
Fixes #105752

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users talking to an assistant would see the model's internal deliberation in the reply when the model emits its chain of thought as plain text in the answer body (a leading `Reasoning:` block with continuation lines) instead of using the structured reasoning channel. Tag-based stripping does not match this shape, so the thinking is rendered on every user-visible surface: final answers, streaming updates, and the message tool. In deployments where the assistant talks to end customers, this is content exposure, not just noise.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds `stripPlainTextReasoningBlock()` and applies it on the three user-visible assistant-text paths. It removes a leading plain-text reasoning block including the italic continuation lines these models emit, and deliberately protects code fences: a fenced block that merely begins with the word "Reasoning" is left untouched. It is a no-op when no such block is present.

Boundary / non-goal: this is output sanitization, not provider-side normalization. If maintainers consider the correct fix to live in provider normalization instead, that is a reasonable call and we are happy to move or close this — we can carry the patch downstream. Opening it because the leak is real and the fix is small and covered by tests.

## User Impact

End users see the answer instead of the model's reasoning preamble, matching the guarantee that already holds for tag-delimited reasoning. No behavior change for models that use the structured channel.

target.title: fix(agents): prevent duplicate subagent recovery after restart
target.body:
Closes #103724

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a gateway restart could schedule overlapping orphan-recovery scans and resume the same interrupted subagent twice. Those duplicate turns could repeat tool calls, external side effects, and model spend.

## Why This Change Was Made

The recovery scheduler now owns one retry chain at a time and coalesces overlapping requests into one follow-up scan. This preserves recovery requests raised while a scan is active without allowing independent scans to dispatch the same orphan concurrently.

The regression parks the first gateway resume, schedules a second recovery request, and verifies that only one resume is dispatched before the first completes and that the queued follow-up observes the cleared restart marker.

Interrupted subagents are resumed at most once across overlapping restart-time recovery triggers, avoiding duplicate work and side effects while retaining a follow-up pass for newly discovered orphaned work.
